original_question: For k >= 3, let D_{k,2}(x, h) = sum_{n<=x} d_k(n) d_2(n+h), and let M_{k,2}(x, h) denote the main term in the known asymptotic formula. Prove an omega theorem for the error D_{k,2}(x, h) - M_{k,2}(x, h).
target_in_paper: Section "Additive divisor sums/shifted convolution sums", Problem (25): Topacogullari [68], [70] and Drappeau [33] have proven asymptotic formulae for D_{k,2}(x,h); prove an omega theorem for D_{k,2}(x,h)-M_{k,2}(x,h) for k >= 3, where M_{k,2}(x,h) is the main term in the asymptotic formula. ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact object D_{k,2}(x,h), the restriction k >= 3, the main-term notation M_{k,2}(x,h), and the goal of proving an omega theorem for the error term. In substance, it is almost verbatim the paper's Problem (25). ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))
missing_details: The paper's notation fixes the domain variables explicitly: x > 0 and h in N, with D_{k,l}(x,h)=sum_{n<=x} d_k(n)d_l(n+h). ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))

The divisor function d_k is defined by zeta(s)^k = sum_{n>=1} d_k(n)/n^s for k > 0; your draft assumes this but does not state it. ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))

A paper-faithful stand-alone version should say that M_{k,2}(x,h) is the main term in the asymptotic formulae proved by Topacogullari [68], [70] and Drappeau [33], because that provenance is part of the official problem statement. ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))

The problem is intended as x -> infinity; your draft does not explicitly state the limiting variable. This is implicit in the phrase 'omega theorem' and in the asymptotic-formula context. ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))

The paper leaves the admissible h-range implicit through the cited asymptotic formulae. A fully stand-alone question should therefore say 'for shifts h in the range where those asymptotic formulae are known'. Nearby Problem (26) shows one concrete such regime for k=3, namely 1 <= h << x^(2/3). ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))

The phrase 'omega theorem' is not further specified in the paper, so a maximally explicit version should clarify whether one seeks an Omega, Omega_+, Omega_-, or two-sided omega result for the error term. ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))
refined_question: Let k >= 3 be an integer, let d_k be the k-th divisor function defined by zeta(s)^k = sum_{n>=1} d_k(n)/n^s, and for x > 0 and h in N define D_{k,2}(x,h) = sum_{n<=x} d_k(n)d_2(n+h). In the ranges of the shift h for which the asymptotic formulae of Topacogullari and Drappeau are known, write D_{k,2}(x,h) = M_{k,2}(x,h) + E_{k,2}(x,h), where M_{k,2}(x,h) denotes the corresponding main term. Prove an omega theorem, as x -> infinity, for the error term E_{k,2}(x,h) = D_{k,2}(x,h) - M_{k,2}(x,h). ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))
justification: This paper is a problem list, and the draft matches an explicit open problem rather than a theorem or conjecture with a numbered statement. The exact match is Problem (25) in the section "Additive divisor sums/shifted convolution sums". The Notation section supplies the precise definitions of d_k and D_{k,l}(x,h). Nearby Problem (26) confirms the intended local context for M_{k,2}(x,h): in the case D_{3,2}(x,h), the main term is written as xP_3(log x) with h-dependent coefficients, so the paper is clearly asking for an omega result for the error in an already known asymptotic formula, not for a new asymptotic formula itself. ([personal.math.ubc.ca](https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~gerg/papers/downloads/MLPL.pdf))
